The trade exchange between Venezuela and Colombia surpassed $1.017 billion in the first nine months of 2026, marking an annual increase of 33.6% in September alone, with figures reaching $144.98 million, according to data released this Friday by the Colombian-Venezuelan Chamber.

From January to September, Colombian exports to Venezuela totaled $938.84 million—an increase of 20.4%—while imports from Venezuela amounted to $79.10 million, reflecting a decline of 5%.

The binational chamber noted that the progress in trade creates favorable conditions to move beyond mere buying and selling of goods. "Colombia and Venezuela have the opportunity to develop joint investments, strengthen value chains, and take advantage of the complementarity of their economies," said Felipe González, the president of the entity's board of directors.

ANNOUNCEMENT

The current performance contrasts sharply with the severe contraction experienced after the historic peak of over $7 billion reached in 2008, when Venezuela was Colombia's second-largest trading partner.

The diplomatic tensions between the administrations of Juan Manuel Santos and Iván Duque with Nicolás Maduro, along with the closure of border crossings ordered in 2015 and the rupture of relations in February 2019, caused formal trade flows to plummet to a low of $222 million in 2020.

Progressive recovery began following the normalization of diplomatic relations and the reopening of borders for cargo transport, finalized on September 26, 2022, during Gustavo Petro's administration. Since then, bilateral trade has risen from $728 million in 2022 to $791 million in 2023 and $1.124 billion in 2024, closing at $1.170 billion at the end of 2025.

With information from EFE

Oil prices closed higher, fluctuating throughout the session on Friday, the 20th, but marked the third consecutive week of decline due to increased exports from the Middle East. The high volume of oil transport contrasts with the ongoing attacks by the Houthis from Yemen and Iran's offensive against vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

Follow the Correio Braziliense channel on WhatsApp to receive the day's top news on your mobile.

Traded on the New York Mercantile Exchange (Nymex), West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude for January settled up 1.18% ($0.97) at $83.41 per barrel. Brent crude for the same month, traded on the Intercontinental Exchange in London (ICE), ended the day up 0.64% ($0.59) at $92.57 per barrel. For the week, WTI and Brent fell by 5.81% and 3.39%, respectively.

Stay updated on the news that matters to you!

This comes according to analysts from the Australian investment bank Macquarie. "The persistence of the status quo with Iran's blockade and convoys through the Strait could maintain pressure on oil markets, but we cannot completely rule out the potential for escalation," they state.

According to Brown Brothers Harriman (BBH), oil flow in the Persian Gulf is currently at about 80% of pre-war levels, which is expected to lead to a decrease in gasoline and diesel prices. The American bank also highlights that the main takeaway for the market from the U.S.-Russia-China Leaders' Declaration was the commitment to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products.

Nevertheless, tensions continue in the Middle East. The Houthis fired missiles at Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, hitting one of the kingdom's most prominent landmarks. In the Strait of Hormuz, two oil tankers hit naval mines and "are on fire," according to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

President Donald Trump stated today that Iran wants to end the war in the Middle East but does not seek an "acceptable" deal for the Republican. The White House chief reiterated that the Persian regime will never have a nuclear weapon.

By Agência Estado

By Theodore Littleton

BOSTON, Nov 20 (IFR) -

Click the PDF icon above for the full version of The Week Ahead in U.S. Economics, including select economic indicator previews.

The week of November 23–27 features a good number of data releases, with the Thanksgiving holiday compressing them into the first few days of the week. The key releases will include the preliminary S&P Global Manufacturing and Services PMIs on Monday; the Conference Board’s Consumer Confidence Index on Tuesday; and the October durable goods and Personal Income and Outlays reports on Wednesday. Filling out the week will be the Chicago Fed National Activity Index on Monday; the Philadelphia Fed Nonmanufacturing Business Outlook Survey, S&P Global and FHFA house price indices, and the Richmond Fed business surveys on Tuesday; the second look at Q3 GDP, weekly jobless claims, and new home sales on Wednesday; and the Advance Economic Indicators report on Friday.

As usual for a holiday week, there is little Fedspeak, with the only speaker currently scheduled being FRB New York President Williams (voter, centrist) in a conversation at University of Mount Saint Vincent on Monday. The Fed will release a new Beige Book report on Wednesday, however, providing context for discussions at the December FOMC meeting.

New Delhi

New Delhi, Nov. 21 -- Petrol and diesel prices today, November 21: Petrol and diesel prices have remained largely steady across major cities despite a surge in global crude oil costs due to the US-Iran war, which led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Union Petroleum and Natural Gas Minister Hardeep Singh Puri attributed this to the Centre's strategy of cutting excise duties and managing domestic fuel supplies.

Petrol and diesel prices rose by 50-60% in several countries, while India managed to keep domestic retail rates relatively stable, Puri said, noting that the government has shielded Indian consumers from the full impact of international fuel price volatility.

The latest cut reduced central excise duty on both petrol and diesel by Rs.10 per litre.

Global crude oil prices have been hovering around $92 per barrel, up from around $67-68 per barrel pre-disruption.

Here is a look at the petrol and diesel prices in major metropolitan cities as of November 21:

New Delhi: Petrol is retailing at Rs.102.12 per litre, while diesel is priced at Rs.95.20 per litre. The national capital continues to have relatively lower fuel prices compared to other metros.

Mumbai: In the financial capital, petrol is priced at Rs.111.21 per litre, and diesel costs Rs.97.83 per litre.

Chennai: Residents in Chennai are paying Rs.107.76 per litre for petrol and Rs.99.55 per litre for diesel.

Kolkata: Petrol costs Rs.113.51 per litre, while diesel costs Rs.99.82 per litre.

Bengaluru: Petrol is priced at Rs.110.44 per litre, and diesel at Rs.99.56 per litre.

Hyderabad: Petrol costs Rs.116.15 per litre, while diesel costs Rs.104.23 per litre.

India's crude oil imports rose around 4.7% in October from the previous month to 23.31 million metric tons, data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell showed. On an annual basis, crude oil imports were up around 11% from 21 million tons in October last year.

Imports of oil products fell 2.8% in October from September, and were down about 41% from a year earlier. Product exports were up 4.7% from October 2025, to 5.36 million tons, the data revealed.

Meanwhile, Reliance Industries Ltd increased imports of Russian oil by 9.6% from September to 393,500 barrels per day (bpd) in October, according to data from industry and trade sources.

India's fuel consumption in October rose nearly 10% from the previous month to 20.49 million metric tons, its highest level since March, according to data from earlier this month. Washington, United States. Oil prices rose slightly on Friday, caught between fears of an escalation in the Middle East and the prospect of significant volumes of crude oil entering the market in the coming months.

North Sea Brent crude for January delivery gained 0.64%, reaching $92.57.

Its U.S. counterpart, West Texas Intermediate crude for December delivery, increased by 0.93% to $83.98.

"It is still too early to consider the crisis over" in the Middle East, warns John Kilduff, an analyst at Again Capital, in comments to AFP. "We remain on a rollercoaster between war and peace."

Saudi forces indicated on Friday that they had carried out a series of attacks in Yemen, particularly targeting a port controlled by Iran-backed Houthi forces.

The Houthis threatened to attack Saudi ports and the financial district of Riyadh, in a conflict with no clear resolution in sight. Attacks or announcements of bombings occur almost daily between both sides since October.

Attacks in Yemen and uncertainty over a potential new offensive against Iran have pressured the market, although expectations of oversupply have limited crude oil's rise (TOBIAS SCHWARZ/AFP)

They specifically target oil infrastructures, raising concerns about disruptions in crude supply.

Meanwhile, operators continue to scrutinize negotiations between Washington and Tehran, with no signs of progress for the time being.

U.S. President Donald Trump, however, told the American outlet Axios that he is in no rush to attack Iran again, contrary to previous reports suggesting a resumption of bombings.

"I'm not in a hurry to make a decision (on Iran). We'll see what happens after the start of the year," the President said in a phone call to Axios from Air Force One, returning from a summit he attended in China.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday, citing U.S. and Israeli officials, that Donald Trump was considering a new bombing campaign against Iran, as Israel pressures Washington to act.

The rise in oil prices remained moderate on Friday, as markets continue to anticipate a potential oversupply in the final quarter of 2026.

6.1 Activities

Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste SAB de CV (ASUR), a leading airport operator in Mexico, manages and develops a network of airports primarily in the southeastern region, including key hubs like Cancun International Airport. Its core business revolves around aeronautical services, such as passenger and cargo handling, alongside non-aeronautical activities including retail, advertising, and real estate development within airport facilities. ASUR has experienced robust growth in international passenger traffic, driven by the surge in tourism to popular destinations like Cancun and the Riviera Maya, which has become one of its fastest-expanding segments. Additionally, commercial revenue streams from airport concessions and enhanced infrastructure projects, such as terminal expansions and digital services, have fueled this momentum. Operating under a concession model, ASUR focuses on efficiency and sustainability to capitalize on Mexico's rising air travel demand, positioning the company as a vital player in the country's aviation sector. It is Mexico's 2nd largest Engineering & construction company by market capitalization.

6.1 Activities

Grupo Aeroportuario del Pacifico SAB de CV is a prominent Mexican airport operator, managing a network of 12 airports primarily in the country's Pacific region, including key hubs like Guadalajara, Puerto Vallarta, and Los Cabos. The company's core business centers on the development, operation, and maintenance of airport infrastructure, encompassing passenger handling, cargo services, and commercial activities such as retail concessions, parking, and advertising. This diversified revenue stream supports efficient air travel and logistics, contributing to Mexico's tourism and trade sectors.

The fastest-growing segments include international passenger traffic, driven by rising tourism and business travel to resort destinations, as well as cargo operations fueled by e-commerce expansion and global supply chain demands. Additionally, non-aeronautical revenues from enhanced retail and dining options in terminals have seen significant growth, reflecting the company's strategic investments in infrastructure modernization and customer experience improvements. Overall, GAP plays a vital role in fostering regional connectivity and economic development in western Mexico. It is Mexico's largest Engineering & construction company by market capitalization.

The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation (SCJN) upheld a fine of 18.4 million pesos imposed on Buenavista del Cobre, a subsidiary of Grupo México, due to environmental violations detected during 2022 and 2023. On Thursday, the Court's presiding minister, Hugo Aguilar Ortiz, dismissed the last appeal filed by the company, determining that the case did not present an exceptional legal interest justifying its review. This decision solidified the sanction from the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa), whose validity had previously been confirmed by the Federal Administrative Justice Tribunal (TFJA). The notification published in the SCJN's electronic notices indicates that the appeal would not establish a relevant legal precedent for the national legal framework. It also specifies that no further means of appeal are available against the order rejecting the review in direct amparo.

WHY WAS BUENAVISTA DEL COBRE FINED?. One of the main irregularities cited by the environmental authority was that, in 2022, Buenavista del Cobre recorded 613,218 metric tons of dry copper and molybdenum concentrate, exceeding the authorized annual limit of 540,000 tons. The company argued that part of the material was recirculated during the production process, and therefore should not be considered as additional volume. However, this argument did not refute Profepa's findings.

The penalty was also related to non-compliance in noise measurements and the operation of equipment without the necessary authorization.

PROFEPA IMPOSED THE SANCTION IN 2024 AND THE TFJA CONFIRMED IT IN 2025. Profepa issued the sanctioning resolution on July 31, 2024. In addition to the financial penalties, the determination included a temporary closure of equipment and the implementation of corrective measures. Buenavista del Cobre challenged the resolution on September 9, 2024. However, on March 5, 2025, the Federal Administrative Justice Tribunal confirmed the validity of the sanction. The company took the case to the Supreme Court through a final review appeal, which was dismissed by the presiding minister. As a result, the fine of 18.4 million pesos was upheld.

Se añade un comentario de AT&T

CIUDAD DE MÉXICO, 20 nov (Reuters) - Los usuarios de telefonía móvil mexicanos informaron el viernes de cortes generalizados en el servicio que afectaron a Telcel, AT&T T.N México y Movistar, lo que supone la última interrupción en las redes móviles del país.

Los usuarios comenzaron a informar de problemas alrededor de las 11 de la mañana, hora local, entre los que se incluían la imposibilidad de realizar llamadas, la pérdida de señal móvil y problemas para acceder a los datos móviles, según la plataforma de seguimiento de interrupciones Downdetector.

  • Telcel está controlada por América Móvil AMXB.MX, mientras que Movistar sigue siendo operada por la española Telefónica TEF.MC, aunque su venta al consorcio estadounidense Melisa Acquisition está en curso

  • Los portavoces de América Móvil y Movistar no respondieron de inmediato a las solicitudes de comentarios

  • AT&T México afirmó que su red «funcionaba con normalidad» y que cualquier dificultad para comunicarse con clientes de otros operadores se debía «a motivos ajenos a nuestra red».

  • La Comisión Reguladora de las Telecomunicaciones de México (CRT) tampoco respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de Reuters

  • Esta interrupción se produce poco más de un mes después de que los usuarios informaran de cortes a mediados de octubre, entre los que se incluían la pérdida de señal móvil y problemas con las llamadas y los datos móviles

Adds comment from AT&T

MEXICO CITY, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Mexican cellphone users reported widespread service outages on Friday affecting Telcel, AT&T T.N Mexico and Movistar, marking the latest disruption to mobile networks in the country.

Users began reporting problems around 11 a.m. local time, including an inability to make calls, loss of cellular signal and problems accessing mobile data, according to outage-tracking platform Downdetector.

  • Telcel is controlled by America Movil AMXB.MX, while Movistar remains operated by Spain's Telefonica TEF.MC while its sale to US consortium Melisa Acquisition is underway

  • Spokespeople for America Movil and Movistar did not immediately respond to requests for comment

  • AT&T Mexico said its network was "operating normally" and that any difficulties communicating with customers from other carriers were "due to reasons unrelated to our network"

  • Mexico's Commission for Telecommunications Regulation (CRT) also did not immediately respond to a Reuters request

  • The disruption comes just over a month after users reported outages in mid-October including loss of cellular signal and problems with calls and mobile data

(Reporting by Kylie Madry, Raul Cortes, Stefanie Eschenbacher and Lizbeth Diaz; Editing by Natalia Siniawski and Iñigo Alexander)

Users began reporting problems around 11 a.m. local time, including an inability to make calls, loss of cellular signal and problems accessing mobile data, according to outage-tracking platform Downdetector.

• Telcel is controlled by America Movil AMXB.MX, while Movistar remains operated by Spain's Telefonica TEF.MC while its sale to US consortium Melisa Acquisition is underway

• Spokespeople for America Movil and Movistar did not immediately respond to requests for comment

• AT&T Mexico said its network was "operating normally" and that any difficulties communicating with customers from other carriers were "due to reasons unrelated to our network"

• Mexico's Commission for Telecommunications Regulation (CRT) also did not immediately respond to a Reuters request

• The disruption comes just over a month after users reported outages in mid-October including loss of cellular signal and problems with calls and mobile data

(Reporting by Kylie Madry, Raul Cortes, Stefanie Eschenbacher and Lizbeth Diaz; Editing by Natalia Siniawski and Iñigo Alexander)

  • Markets await Lula's pick for finance minister
  • BofA sees scope for renewed capital inflows into Brazil
  • Mexican retail sales signal softer domestic demand

By Tharuniyaa Lakshmi

Nov 20 (Reuters) - Latin American equities fell to over one-year lows on Friday as a global equity selloff intensified after Anthropic's IPO failed to restore confidence in the AI sector, while prospects of higher US interest rates kept pressure on regional currencies.

While Latin American markets have limited direct exposure to the technology sector, the deterioration in global risk sentiment spilled over into the region.

MSCI's index of Latin American equities .MILA00000PUS fell 0.86%, while the corresponding currency gauge .MILA00000CUS fell 1.5% and was on track for its fourth consecutive weekly loss.

Markets in the region's largest economy, Brazil, were closed for a holiday. The Brazilian real BRL= was down 0.24% against the US dollar on Friday on very low volume.

However, investors monitored domestic developments. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is nearing a decision on his next finance minister, with an announcement possible as early as next week, according to six sources familiar with the discussions.‌

Separately, Bank of America said there remains a potential path for capital inflows to return to Latin America's largest economy despite a challenging economic environment at home and abroad.

MEXICO TRADE HOPES RISE; COMMODITIES RETREAT

In Mexico, the peso was up 0.29%. Investors took note of a potentially positive development on the trade front as EU agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen said he expects Mexico to clear the final hurdle for a new EU trade pact to take effect by the end of the year, bringing Mexican and European interests closer together.

Meanwhile, Mexican retail sales fell in September from the previous month, data from the national statistics agency showed, pointing to softer consumer demand despite remaining higher than a year ago.

Broader global factors also weighed on sentiment. Commodity prices fell, with gold XAU= down 2% and copper was headed for its biggest weekly drop in 19 months.

Chile's peso CLP= fell 0.29% against the dollar, while Peru's sol PEN= slipped 0.15%.‌

Brent crude fell around 1% as concerns over supply disruptions eased, with exports from the Middle East remaining resilient despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Separately, Polish central banker Joanna Tyrowicz told PAP News Agency that interest rates should be "much higher" and that the central bank's communication should remain "hawkish".‌

• Markets await Lula's pick for finance minister
• BofA sees scope for renewed capital inflows into Brazil
• Mexican retail sales signal softer domestic demand
By Tharuniyaa Lakshmi

Nov 20 (Reuters) - Latin American equities fell to over one-year lows on Friday as a global equity selloff intensified after Anthropic's IPO failed to restore confidence in the AI sector, while prospects of higher US interest rates kept pressure on regional currencies.

While Latin American markets have limited direct exposure to the technology sector, the deterioration in global risk sentiment spilled over into the region.

MSCI's index of Latin American equities .MILA00000PUS fell 0.86%, while the corresponding currency gauge .MILA00000CUS fell 1.5% and was on track for its fourth consecutive weekly loss.

Markets in the region's largest economy, Brazil, were closed for a holiday. The Brazilian real BRL= was down 0.24% against the US dollar on Friday on very low volume.

However, investors monitored domestic developments. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is nearing a decision on his next finance minister, with an announcement possible as early as next week, according to six sources familiar with the discussions.‌

Separately, Bank of America said there remains a potential path for capital inflows to return to Latin America's largest economy despite a challenging economic environment at home and abroad.

MEXICO TRADE HOPES RISE; COMMODITIES RETREAT

In Mexico, the peso was up 0.29%. Investors took note of a potentially positive development on the trade front as EU agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen said he expects Mexico to clear the final hurdle for a new EU trade pact to take effect by the end of the year, bringing Mexican and European interests closer together.

Meanwhile, Mexican retail sales fell in September from the previous month, data from the national statistics agency showed, pointing to softer consumer demand despite remaining higher than a year ago.

Broader global factors also weighed on sentiment. Commodity prices fell, with gold XAU= down 2% and copper was headed for its biggest weekly drop in 19 months.

Chile's peso CLP= fell 0.29% against the dollar, while Peru's sol PEN= slipped 0.15%.‌

Brent crude fell around 1% as concerns over supply disruptions eased, with exports from the Middle East remaining resilient despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Separately, Polish central banker Joanna Tyrowicz told PAP News Agency that interest rates should be "much higher" and that the central bank's communication should remain "hawkish".‌

The total number of shares ultimately repurchased under the new ASR agreement will be based on the daily volume-weighted average price of the Companys ADSs during the term of the agreement, less a discount. Sep 09, 2026: Derek Gaskins Takes Marketing Helm at OXXO USA

Derek Gaskins is set to re-enter the convenience-store sector, joining OXXO USA as vice president of marketing and category management. The move will take effect in mid-September, 2026, specifically on the 13th of that month, as Gaskins confirmed in an interview with CSP Daily News.

In his new position at OXXO USA, a subsidiary of Fomento Economico Mexicano, S.A.B. de C.V. (FEMSA), Gaskins will play a pivotal role in shaping the brand's commercial strategy in the U.S. market. He will report directly to CEO Jaime Longoria and oversee a wide array of functions including marketing, merchandising, foodservice, brand development, and supplier partnerships. Gaskins expressed enthusiasm for the role, stating, 'It's one of the most exciting scopes I've had in my career.'

OXXO, which boasts over 26,000 stores globally, has recently made its foray into the United States, acquiring 249 stores from Delek US in October 2024. As OXXO seeks to build a neighborhood-relevant, food-forward convenience experience, Gaskins is expected to harness his extensive industry experience to drive growth. He noted, 'They are trying to build something meaningful here—and they asked me to help lead that commercial effort.'

Prior to this role, Gaskins held positions at Hotel Chocolat and bp, where he focused on enhancing customer experience and operational efficiency. His background includes significant tenures at various convenience retail brands, positioning him as a seasoned leader in the sector. Gaskins remarked, 'OXXO represents something I could not responsibly say no to,' highlighting the strategic importance of this opportunity.

As OXXO USA prepares to establish a stronger foothold in the U.S., Gaskins emphasized the brand's commitment to earning its place in the market. He noted, 'FEMSA came to stay, and they are bringing global best practices, significant capital, and a proven operating model.' With Gaskins at the helm of marketing, OXXO USA is poised to become a serious contender in the competitive convenience store landscape.

Moyobamba, Tarapoto, and Trujillo are the cities in Peru that recorded the lowest unemployment rates during the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest report from the National Institute of Statistics and Informatics (INEI), based on the National Employment Permanent Survey (EPEN).

The ranking is led by Moyobamba, with an unemployment rate of 2.2%. It is followed by Tarapoto at 2.5% and Trujillo at 2.9%. Other cities that stood out for their low rates include Iquitos (3.1%), Pucallpa (3.8%), Puerto Maldonado (3.9%), and Arequipa (3.9%).

Also noted are Abancay (4%), Chachapoyas (4%), Bagua Grande (4.1%), and Cusco (4.2%). Meanwhile, Metropolitan Lima and Callao recorded an unemployment rate of 4.4%.

Which cities have the highest unemployment?

At the opposite end of the report, Cajamarca presented the highest unemployment rate at 10%. It is followed by Moquegua (8.5%), Chimbote (8.1%), Huancavelica (7.7%), and Cerro de Pasco (6.6%).

Additionally, high rates were reported in Chiclayo (6.4%), Puno (6.3%), Juliaca (5.9%), Tumbes (5.7%), and both Piura and Ayacucho (5.6% each), according to Andina.

Nationally, the unemployment rate reached 4% during the third quarter of 2026, representing a reduction of 0.3 percentage points compared to the same period in 2025, when it stood at 4.3%.

Informal employment: cities with the highest rates

The INEI report also highlights significant differences in labor informality. Between October 2025 and September 2026, Juliaca recorded the highest rate of informal employment at 81.8%. It was followed by Pucallpa (74.9%), Bagua Grande (74.1%), Ayacucho (71%), and Tumbes (70.6%).

In contrast, Metropolitan Lima and Callao presented an informality rate of 53.4%, while Ica and Moquegua recorded 54%, respectively. Informal employment includes labor activities that do not have social protection or the benefits established by law.

Coca-Cola FEMSA, S.A.B. de C.V. has unveiled its new 2.5L Returnable PET Bottle, targeting family consumption in key Mexican markets. This launch, taking place on 23rd June 2026, is a significant step in the company's strategy to enhance the availability of reusable packaging solutions.

The Coca-Cola FEMSA 2.5L Returnable PET Bottle is designed for households that prefer purchasing beverages in bulk while maintaining the option for return and reuse. This innovative format not only aims to reduce packaging waste but also lowers the per-liter cost for consumers, who can return the bottle to local corner stores, which have long embraced returnable formats.

Mariana Rodriguez, product manager at Coca-Cola FEMSA, noted that the bottle features a more pronounced waist and a textured grip, enhancing usability at family gatherings. The design is lighter than traditional glass returnable bottles, making it easier for all family members, including children and seniors, to handle. While glass maintains a nostalgic appeal, the PET format provides a modern balance of convenience and tradition.

Coca-Cola FEMSA's CEO, John Santa Maria, has emphasized the importance of refillable packaging as a core strategy. The new 2.5L Returnable PET Bottle aligns with the company's sustainability goals, as using refillable containers can significantly reduce the carbon footprint associated with beverage consumption. This initiative not only supports environmental efforts but also fosters a culture of reuse among consumers.

Initially available in select Mexican markets, the Coca-Cola FEMSA 2.5L Returnable PET Bottle leverages the existing popularity of refillable formats. The pricing structure typically includes a deposit for the bottle, making it economically advantageous for families who purchase large quantities. This strategic move is expected to positively impact Coca-Cola FEMSA's long-term cash flow and shareholder value, as the company continues to adapt to consumer preferences while committing to sustainable practices.

Jun 17, 2026: Coca-Cola FEMSA Leverages Logistics-as-a-Service to Enhance Distribution

Coca-Cola FEMSA, S.A.B. de C.V. is quietly enhancing its distribution capabilities through Fomento Economico Mexicano's Logistics-as-a-Service offering. This innovative service transforms FEMSA's robust Coca-Cola delivery network into a third-party logistics solution for brands requiring efficient, temperature-controlled distribution across Mexico. This strategic move was made public on the 17th of June, 2026, and is expected to reshape the logistical landscape in the region.

FEMSA's Logistics-as-a-Service fundamentally allows third-party brands to access the same warehousing, routing software, and last-mile fleet utilized by Coca-Cola in Mexico and other Latin American markets. Clients can seamlessly integrate into FEMSA's extensive delivery network, which significantly reduces the need for them to establish their own complex logistics operations. This means that consumer goods can be efficiently delivered to over 3 million points of sale, utilizing existing routes that serve thousands of small retail outlets daily.

For brands, especially those in the fast-moving consumer goods sector, this service provides an invaluable shortcut to market penetration. Products delivered alongside Coca-Cola benefit from the established distribution patterns that store owners are accustomed to, thus facilitating easier acceptance and integration into existing supply chains. The service's reach can substantially expedite market entry for new energy drinks or healthcare products, compressing lengthy rollout periods into mere months.

Technological infrastructure underpins this service, with advanced routing algorithms and inventory management tools ensuring efficient operations. FEMSA's Logistics-as-a-Service also offers clients features such as order tracking and delivery proof without necessitating additional investment in software. This is particularly crucial for pharmaceuticals and health products, where stringent temperature control and delivery reliability are essential.

Logistics-as-a-Service is a strategic component of FEMSA's broader vision to maximize value from its existing infrastructure. Although still a smaller segment compared to its core Coca-Cola bottling and OXXO retail operations, it represents a significant opportunity for growth. Investors should note that while immediate scale may be limited, the long-term potential for operating leverage in this logistics venture aligns with FEMSA's overarching objective of enhancing its distribution capabilities.

Technological infrastructure underpins this service, with advanced routing algorithms and inventory management tools ensuring efficient operations. Jul 20, 2026: Grupo Financiero Banorte's Growth Strategy Emphasizes Sustainability and Innovation

In an exclusive interview, Mr. Jose Luis Munoz, Executive Director of Sustainability & Investor Relations at Grupo Financiero Banorte, outlined the bank's strategic position for sustainable growth. The discussion, held on the 20th of July 2026, highlighted Banorte's financial performance amid a dynamic economic landscape and its commitment to fostering long-term sustainability.

Reflecting on Banorte's 125-year legacy, Munoz emphasized that the definition of a strong bank has evolved with changing economic and geopolitical landscapes. 'Resilience has been a hallmark of Banorte's history,' he explained, noting the bank's ability to navigate various challenges, including the rise of fintech competitors and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. This resilience is evident in the bank's growing loan portfolio, particularly in consumer lending, which saw an increase in mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards.

The bank's commitment to the SME sector remains a cornerstone of its strategy, with dedicated resources aimed at improving customer interaction and service. Munoz explained that Banorte's extensive branch network, particularly in economically active regions, positions it favorably to cater to the needs of SMEs. The bank's approach to 'hyper-personalisation' through advanced technology and analytics further differentiates it from competitors, allowing for tailored offerings that resonate with customer needs.

Banorte's financial health is underscored by a robust capital adequacy ratio of 20.06%, well above regulatory requirements. Munoz highlighted the importance of maintaining a safety buffer due to the bank's status as a systemic institution without foreign subsidiaries. This focus on capital preservation, coupled with disciplined risk management, has enabled Banorte to sustain its strong liquidity position and support growth initiatives.

Sustainability is woven into the fabric of Banorte's operations, with initiatives such as the commitment to plant one million trees by 2030 and participation in the Task Force on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD). Munoz noted that these efforts not only enhance the bank's sustainability practices but also help clients navigate risks associated with nature and biodiversity. As Banorte continues to expand its influence in the financial sector, its commitment to innovation, customer experience, and sustainable practices positions it as a key player in Mexico's economic development.

Jul 02, 2026: Grupo Financiero Banorte Strengthens Its Position in Mexico's Banking Sector

Grupo Financiero Banorte continues to position itself as one of Mexico's largest banks, combining a traditional branch network with digital services as it competes for retail and corporate customers in a changing rate and regulatory environment. As of 2nd July 2026, Banorte operates in an environment shaped by domestic interest rates, economic growth, and evolving regulation.

Grupo Financiero Banorte S.A.B. (ISIN MXP370641013) is one of Mexico's largest financial groups, with activities spanning commercial banking, consumer finance, asset management, insurance, and pension funds. As a major lender in the Mexican market, the group plays a central role in financing households and businesses across the country. Its nationwide branch and ATM network supports a wide retail franchise, while its corporate and government banking units provide services to larger clients and public entities.

Management attention at Banorte typically centers on maintaining a balance between growth and risk, especially in areas such as consumer credit, mortgages, and small-business lending. Asset quality indicators, such as non-performing loans and coverage ratios, are closely watched, as they show how well the bank is managing credit risk in its portfolio. Additionally, capital adequacy remains a key concern, with banks expected to hold sufficient capital buffers to absorb potential losses and comply with regulatory requirements.

Banorte has invested in digital channels to complement its traditional branch network, offering online and mobile banking for individuals and businesses. These platforms allow customers to make payments, transfer funds, and apply for products such as credit cards and personal loans without visiting a branch. The ability to migrate more activity to digital channels helps Banorte improve efficiency by reducing operating costs per customer while maintaining or even expanding its customer base.

Banorte's shares are listed in Mexico, providing investors exposure to the country's financial sector through a diversified banking and financial services group. The stock's performance over time reflects local macroeconomic conditions, interest rate trends, and the bank's own profitability and risk management decisions. For equity investors, key variables often include return on equity, cost-to-income ratios, asset growth, and dividend policy, all of which shape how the market values Banorte relative to both domestic peers and international financial groups.

Jul 20, 2026: Grupo Financiero Banorte's Growth Strategy Emphasizes Sustainability and Innovation

In an exclusive interview, Mr. Jose Luis Munoz, Executive Director of Sustainability & Investor Relations at Grupo Financiero Banorte, outlined the bank's strategic position for sustainable growth. The discussion, held on the 20th of July 2026, highlighted Banorte's financial performance amid a dynamic economic landscape and its commitment to fostering long-term sustainability.

Reflecting on Banorte's 125-year legacy, Munoz emphasized that the definition of a strong bank has evolved with changing economic and geopolitical landscapes. 'Resilience has been a hallmark of Banorte's history,' he explained, noting the bank's ability to navigate various challenges, including the rise of fintech competitors and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. This resilience is evident in the bank's growing loan portfolio, particularly in consumer lending, which saw an increase in mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards.

The bank's commitment to the SME sector remains a cornerstone of its strategy, with dedicated resources aimed at improving customer interaction and service. Munoz explained that Banorte's extensive branch network, particularly in economically active regions, positions it favorably to cater to the needs of SMEs. The bank's approach to 'hyper-personalisation' through advanced technology and analytics further differentiates it from competitors, allowing for tailored offerings that resonate with customer needs.

Banorte's financial health is underscored by a robust capital adequacy ratio of 20.06%, well above regulatory requirements. Munoz highlighted the importance of maintaining a safety buffer due to the bank's status as a systemic institution without foreign subsidiaries. This focus on capital preservation, coupled with disciplined risk management, has enabled Banorte to sustain its strong liquidity position and support growth initiatives.

Sustainability is woven into the fabric of Banorte's operations, with initiatives such as the commitment to plant one million trees by 2030 and participation in the Task Force on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD). Munoz noted that these efforts not only enhance the bank's sustainability practices but also help clients navigate risks associated with nature and biodiversity. As Banorte continues to expand its influence in the financial sector, its commitment to innovation, customer experience, and sustainable practices positions it as a key player in Mexico's economic development.

Jul 02, 2026: Grupo Financiero Banorte Strengthens Its Position in Mexico's Banking Sector

Grupo Financiero Banorte continues to position itself as one of Mexico's largest banks, combining a traditional branch network with digital services as it competes for retail and corporate customers in a changing rate and regulatory environment. As of 2nd July 2026, Banorte operates in an environment shaped by domestic interest rates, economic growth, and evolving regulation.

Grupo Financiero Banorte S.A.B. (ISIN MXP370641013) is one of Mexico's largest financial groups, with activities spanning commercial banking, consumer finance, asset management, insurance, and pension funds. As a major lender in the Mexican market, the group plays a central role in financing households and businesses across the country. Its nationwide branch and ATM network supports a wide retail franchise, while its corporate and government banking units provide services to larger clients and public entities.

Management attention at Banorte typically centers on maintaining a balance between growth and risk, especially in areas such as consumer credit, mortgages, and small-business lending. Asset quality indicators, such as non-performing loans and coverage ratios, are closely watched, as they show how well the bank is managing credit risk in its portfolio. Additionally, capital adequacy remains a key concern, with banks expected to hold sufficient capital buffers to absorb potential losses and comply with regulatory requirements.

Banorte has invested in digital channels to complement its traditional branch network, offering online and mobile banking for individuals and businesses. These platforms allow customers to make payments, transfer funds, and apply for products such as credit cards and personal loans without visiting a branch. The ability to migrate more activity to digital channels helps Banorte improve efficiency by reducing operating costs per customer while maintaining or even expanding its customer base.

Banorte's shares are listed in Mexico, providing investors exposure to the country's financial sector through a diversified banking and financial services group. The stock's performance over time reflects local macroeconomic conditions, interest rate trends, and the bank's own profitability and risk management decisions. For equity investors, key variables often include return on equity, cost-to-income ratios, asset growth, and dividend policy, all of which shape how the market values Banorte relative to both domestic peers and international financial groups.

Findings from National University Broaden Understanding of Sustainability Research (Export Competitiveness of Peruvian Andean Grains: Structural Dynamics and Emerging Water-sustainability Considerations, 2015-2024)

2026 NOV 18-- By a News Reporter-Staff News Editor at Ecology Daily News-- Researchers detail new data in Sustainability Research. According to news reporting originating from Trujillo, Peru, by NewsRx correspondents, research stated," Quinoa, kiwicha and ca& ntilde; ihua are strategic Andean grains for Peru, yet whether Peru' s revealed comparative advantage in... 2026 NOV 18 (NewsRx) -- By a News Reporter-Staff News Editor at Ecology Daily News -- Researchers detail new data in Sustainability Research. According to news reporting originating from Trujillo, Peru, by NewsRx correspondents, research stated, "Quinoa, kiwicha and ca & ntilde;ihua are strategic Andean grains for Peru, yet whether Peru's revealed comparative advantage in them has translated into export performance remains poorly documented. Using official MINCETUR/SUNAT and International Trade Centre data for 2015-2024 (ten annual observations), this study applies a deliberately descriptive, historical design based on compound annual growth rates (CAGR), historically delimited sub-periods, volatility measures, unit values and the revealed comparative advantage indices RCA and ARCA."

Our news editors obtained a quote from the research from National University, "Quinoa export volume grew at a CAGR of 2.96%, but growth slowed from 12.0% per year in 2015-2017 to 0.5% per year in 2017-2024, while its unit value fell by 28.3% and its export value remained below the 2015 level. Kiwicha and ca & ntilde;ihua showed rising RCA (+40.2% and +70.0%) but very volatile exports (standard deviation of annual growth of 52.3 and 39.5 percentage points) and falling unit values. In all three grains, stable or rising revealed specialisation coexisted with declining export value, a pattern consistent with a 'comparative advantage trap'. Single-site evidence from Puno on the blue water footprint is treated as exploratory."

According to the news editors, the research concluded: "Comparative advantage alone has not secured export competitiveness; differentiation, market diversification and better data are needed."

For more information on this research see: Export Competitiveness of Peruvian Andean Grains: Structural Dynamics and Emerging Water-sustainability Considerations, 2015-2024. Sustainability , 2026;18(20). Sustainability can be contacted at: Mdpi, Mdpi Ag, Grosspeteranlage 5, Ch-4052 Basel, Switzerland.

The news editors report that additional information may be obtained by contacting Heyner Yuliano Marquez Yauri, National University Trujillo, Fac Econ Sci, Profess Sch Adm, Dept. of Administration, Trujillo 13001, Peru. Additional authors for this research include Sandra Lizzette Leon Luyo, Carlos Enrique Cruzado Paredes, Maria Patricia Rodriguez Kong, Catalina Alcira Ramos Laiza, Sergio Antonio Samanamud Pinedo, Manuel Edward Cosme Urbina, Denis Guizela Chavez Bejarano, Jose Alfredo Castaneda Nassi and Aurelio Maximino Carranza Rodriguez.

The direct object identifier (DOI) for that additional information is: https://doi.org/10.3390/su182010676 . This DOI is a link to an online electronic document that is either free or for purchase, and can be your direct source for a journal article and its citation.

The conflict between Cerro Matoso and Canacol Energy over natural gas supply has put the mining company's operations in jeopardy, as it has seen contracted deliveries from the producer progressively decline to nearly zero.

According to figures provided by the company, supply dropped from 16 million cubic feet per day to 11 million in February 226 and subsequently to seven million. By November, deliveries fell to about 3 cubic feet per day, a reduction that forced Cerro Matoso to halt one of its production lines and seek alternatives to ensure continuity of its operations.

This conflict is compounded by the natural gas supply crisis that Colombia is currently facing, amidst the lowest exploratory activity in recent years and the previous government's energy policy decisions led by Gustavo Petro, which did not promote new hydrocarbon exploration contracts.

This situation has increased reliance on the external market: at present, imported gas accounts for 44% of the national supply. In this context, Cerro Matoso's president, Ricardo Gaviria Jansa, explained the difficulties in the industry in an interview with Portafolio.

What is the current situation with Canacol?

Canacol cut us off completely. We had to stop one production line. We ended up at zero because we no longer had the excess gas that Hocol provided.

With the help of the government and other companies, we have managed to secure gas. But I believe the time has come for us to take action.

What do you expect from the Superintendency of Companies' decision regarding the ruling from Canada?

I believe it will be in favor of the industry. Now, whether it comes out in the way we hope—meaning we don't want the 1% that the Canadian Court indicates—I don't think that's going to happen.

The Canadian Court itself stated that if Cerro Matoso's contracts were canceled, there would be a complex public order problem, and that it would have a huge social impact due to the number of people relying on us.

What happens if the Superintendency rules in favor of Cerro Matoso?

I believe that if the Superintendency issues a ruling as we hope and believe it should be, they will have no choice but to stop playing the games they have been playing since this process began.

So, what happens? The search for potential buyers in Canada would have little appetite because they need to proceed with the contracts they currently have.

What they wanted were new contracts with entirely different pricing.

So, in that sense, the National Hydrocarbons Agency will need to define and appoint an operator, which I believe could easily be Hocol or another entity.

What we don't want is for the Canacol well matter to end, as they are currently only producing around 4 to 45 MBTU per day, which is five million cubic feet.

What message are you sending to De La Espriella's Government?

I will tell you one thing; as I have said to everyone: I feel fortunate to meet with government officials at all levels, in all offices, who look at you, listen to you, and discuss matters with you. They say, "This is our position; we are working in a coordinated manner."

However, what happens is that we as an industry would like everything to move faster.

The gas issue has seen four years of neglect.

Before Petro, around 13 gas wells were drilled annually. Under the previous government, only three were drilled on average.

So, there has been a tremendous lack of action.

Today, 4% of the gas is imported.

The latest report states that 44% of the gas used is imported

Every day that passes, the percentage increases by two points, as it was 38% two weeks ago.

Therefore, I believe the message is for continued support, to keep supporting the industry, and to unblock projects.

Because today you cannot impose so much bureaucracy; we need to expedite licenses and permits because drilling is required, and these regasification plants need to start operating as quickly as possible.

Another message is that we need to find ways to prevent abuses in the pricing of the new molecules that will leave the country, as we must not expect that they will be priced at the same value as the imported gas.

This includes Ecopetrol, as it is the largest gas producer in the country.

How much has Cerro Matoso's production fallen, and what has happened with its export markets?

We were supposed to produce 321 tons this year. We will produce 263.

But anticipating all this, we slowed down our sales pace.

So, at this moment, we haven't let anyone down. It would have been worse to breach a contract, which obviously leads to penalties, and clients would not want to see you again.

But we have managed this well with our sales team in Europe and Asia.

What needs to be done now?

The government is doing everything possible to increase drilling.

The Cartagena regasifier, Puerto Bahía, is supposed to be ready by next year, around February or March.

There is another regasifier expected to come online in 2028, which is the Palermo regasifier, in front of the port of Barranquilla. This regasifier is smaller.

Today they are finishing, I believe, finalizing the financial aspects in New York, and construction should begin soon, so it should be ready by 2028.

Additionally, there are some wells and fields in testing. This could generate some interesting gas production.

Industrias Peñoles, the world's leading silver producer, has signed a 20-year renewable energy supply contract with Atlas Renewable Energy, a U.S. company that develops, builds, and operates energy projects in Latin America.

The contract includes the development of a solar generation and storage project located in the state of Coahuila, which is set to commence operations in the first half of 2029. It will feature a peak solar capacity of 269 megawatts and a battery storage system that will collectively supply around 550 gigawatt hours annually.

"The supply will support part of the electricity demand for its operations in the northern part of the country and is part of the company's strategy to enhance the energy competitiveness of its processes and increase the use of renewable sources," Atlas Renewable Energy stated in a press release.

With this agreement, Atlas Renewable Energy will establish its first renewable energy supply contract with a private client in Mexico, thus expanding its client portfolio, which includes leading companies in the mining, metallurgy, chemical, cement, and technology sectors.

"This contract demonstrates that solar energy with storage is a competitive option for large industries in the country, a technology in which Atlas is a leader in Latin America," said Camilo Serrano, the country manager for Mexico at Atlas Renewable Energy, in the same release. "We thank Peñoles for their trust in our development and implementation capabilities, and we look forward to supporting their growth and that of the mining industry in the country."

Since Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's (PT) victory on October 25, the U.S. dollar has increased by 14.8%, and the Brazilian real has recorded the worst performance among the 116 currencies monitored by Austin Rating. This represents the worst currency reaction in the world during this period. The effects of the devaluation are already evident in wholesale markets, where prices have seen the greatest increase in over a year.

According to Jacqueline Neo, head of operations and currency at be.Smart, the devaluation of the real reflects a growing perception of economic risk concerning Brazil.

"The market is attentive to the conduct of fiscal policy, particularly the government's ability to balance revenues and expenditures and to present a sustainable trajectory for public debt," she states.

Fiscal risk pressures inflation expectations

Even with low inflation in October, expectations point to a price acceleration in the coming years. The IPCA (Broad Consumer Price Index) stood at 0.14%, half of the midpoint of financial market projections, according to the Central Bank's Focus Bulletin released a week earlier.

However, inflation expectations for 2027 have risen since the second round of the election. A survey by the Central Bank (BC) with financial institutions indicates that the median projections for the IPCA increased from 4.34% on October 23, before the runoff, to 5% on the last Friday (13).

Stronger dollar increases production costs and reaches store shelves

The devaluation of the real raises production costs for companies that rely on imported inputs and raw materials priced in dollars. As these costs are present at various stages of the production chain, price increases can reach final prices even when the product is made in Brazil.

"The dollar serves as a price reference for a significant portion of the economy. Even products manufactured in Brazil can have costs tied to the U.S. currency, whether due to raw materials, inputs used in production, or transportation. Therefore, a persistent appreciation of the exchange rate can pressure the cost of living for the entire population, regardless of whether individuals have direct dealings with foreign currency," explains Fábio Martini, consultant at Mhydas Financial Planning.

Wholesale prices reach the highest level in over a year

The pressure is already visible in wholesale price indicators. For the 12-month period leading up to November, the Broad Producer Price Index (IPA-10) rose by 5.85%, the highest increase in more than a year, according to the Brazilian Institute of Economics of Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV Ibre).

The indicator has recorded increases for three consecutive months, driven by gasoline, products from the soybean chain, and cattle. The accumulated change over 12 months rose from 2.57% in September to 5.03% in October, reaching 5.85% in November.

The Producer Price Index (IPP), calculated by the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE), also indicates pressure on industrial costs, albeit with a two-month lag. In September, the latest available data, the indicator recorded an increase of 4.34% compared to the same month in 2025.

The currency devaluation may amplify this pressure in the coming months. "With a stronger dollar, imported inputs may further pressure prices, adding between 0.4 to 0.7 percentage points to the IPCA for 2027. Retail and distribution companies, which are facing consumers more sensitive to price adjustments, may see a compression of margins by 1.5 to 3 percentage points," estimates Letícia Moschioni, partner at Finscale.

Fuel, food, and electronics also feel the pressure

Fuels are among the first products to feel the effects of the exchange rate. Since oil is priced in dollars, the devaluation of the real increases the prices of gasoline and diesel, even when there is no change in the international price of crude oil.

To this effect are added tensions in the Middle East, which are pushing oil and its derivative prices higher. The impact extends beyond gas stations: the road transport of goods also becomes more expensive, spreading costs throughout the logistics chain.

In food, imported wheat influences the prices of products such as bread, pasta, and cookies. Meanwhile, chicken and pork production relies on feed made from corn and soybeans, which are also priced in dollars. Fresh produce, for their part, respond to other factors such as El Niño and seasonality, according to economists from XP Investimentos in a report.

The pressure also reaches electronics and appliances, which use imported components. El Niño reduces the draft of the Amazon rivers—the depth available for navigation—and increases shipping costs for production from the Free Trade Zone of Manaus, one of Brazil's main industrial hubs.

With difficulties in transporting goods via waterways, some cargo must resort to air transport, which has also become more expensive. Aviation kerosene (QAV) sold to distributors has increased by 83.7% in the year, reaching R$ 6.69 per liter. This marks the highest price in 2026, according to Petrobras's monthly adjustments.

The increase reflects the international hike in fuel prices, exacerbated by reduced refining capacity in Russia and Ukraine. The diversion of cargo to air transport occurs precisely at a time of high costs, increasing pressure on electronic prices.

Medications follow a different dynamic. The currency fluctuation is passed on to prices more slowly due to sector regulation and annual adjustment cycles.

Dollar pass-through varies by product

The time it takes for the dollar's rise to reach consumers varies by product. Gasoline and diesel may feel the effects within a few weeks. In contrast, processed and industrialized food depends on stock levels and supply contracts, which can delay the pass-through for months.

According to Martini, it is not the price recorded on a single day that determines the impact on consumers' wallets, but rather the duration for which the dollar remains at a high level. It is this possibility of persistent devaluation that the market has begun to price in more intensely.

The effects of the devaluation are already evident in wholesale markets, where prices have seen the greatest increase in over a year.

According to Jacqueline Neo, head of operations and currency at be.Smart, the devaluation of the real reflects a growing perception of economic risk concerning Brazil.

"The market is attentive to the conduct of fiscal policy, particularly the government's ability to balance revenues and expenditures and to present a sustainable trajectory for public debt," she states.

Fiscal risk pressures inflation expectations

Even with low inflation in October, expectations point to a price acceleration in the coming years. The IPCA (Broad Consumer Price Index) stood at 0.14%, half of the midpoint of financial market projections, according to the Central Bank's Focus Bulletin released a week earlier.

However, inflation expectations for 2027 have risen since the second round of the election. A survey by the Central Bank (BC) with financial institutions indicates that the median projections for the IPCA increased from 4.34% on October 23, before the runoff, to 5% on the last Friday (13).

"The dollar serves as a price reference for a significant portion of the economy. The general minimum wage in Mexico could see a significant increase by 2027 , rising from the current 9,582.47 pesos per month to approximately 10,700 pesos .

This projection, supported by the Mexican Institute of Public Accountants (IMCP) , anticipates an adjustment of between 12% and 13% , which would translate into an additional 1,118 pesos per month for workers earning the base salary.

The discussion around the minimum wage increase is gaining national significance, as it directly affects the purchasing power of millions of Mexicans and the economy of businesses.

The annual adjustment is determined by the National Commission of Minimum Wages (Conasami) , which includes representatives from labor, employer, and government sectors.

For 2027, the expectation is that the increase will surpass the inflation rate and maintain the trend of wage recovery observed in recent years.

According to estimates from the IMCP and statements from labor authorities, the new daily minimum could be set between 352 and 355 pesos, consolidating progress towards the six-year goal of ensuring that the minimum wage covers at least 2.5 times the value of the basic basket by 2030.

How is the minimum wage increase defined in Mexico?

The process to determine the minimum wage begins each year with the permanent session of Conasami , which in 2026 will commence negotiations starting on November 26 .

During this time, the labor , employer , and government sectors present their proposals and arguments, considering factors such as annual inflation , economic growth, and the effects of labor reforms, including the reduction of the weekly working hours.

The Mexican Constitution establishes that the minimum wage cannot be increased below the inflation rate, ensuring a real adjustment in workers' income. However, in recent years, wage policy has sought to exceed this legal floor, with double-digit increases aimed at recovering the purchasing power lost in previous decades.

The official resolution regarding the new minimum wage must be published no later than December 1 of each year , to take effect on January 1 of the following year.

What are the proposals from the sectors for 2027?

In the negotiation for the 2027 minimum wage , there are notable differences among the involved sectors:

  • The business sector , represented by organizations like Coparmex , has suggested an increase of between 9% and 9.9% , arguing for the need to maintain competitiveness and avoid excessive inflationary pressures.
  • Trade union organizations , such as CTM and the Congress of Labor , have proposed increases of between 12% and 18% , aiming to accelerate wage recovery and improve workers' living conditions.
  • Conasami , through its president Luis Felipe Munguía Corella, has indicated that the range for discussion is between 10% and 15% , ruling out adjustments lower than double digits.

The IMCP supports the position of an increase of between 12% and 13% , which would set the minimum wage at 10,700 pesos per month in 2027.

What factors influence the adjustment of the minimum wage?

The analysis to define the minimum wage increase considers several key elements:

  • Annual inflation: The increase cannot be less than the recorded inflation rate.
  • Economic growth: The capacity of businesses to absorb the increase without affecting formal employment is evaluated.
  • Reduction of working hours: The potential reduction from 48 to 46 hours per week may elevate operational costs, which is taken into account during negotiations.
  • Purchasing power goal: The federal government aims for the minimum wage to cover 2.5 times the value of the basic basket by 2030.

Furthermore, the wage recovery policy implemented since 2018 has been recognized by national and international organizations, as it has allowed more than 6.6 million people to escape multidimensional poverty, according to studies conducted by Conasami.

What would the minimum wage in the Free Trade Zone of the Northern Border look like?

In the Free Trade Zone of the Northern Border , the minimum wage is higher than in the rest of the country. For 2026, it is set at 440.87 pesos daily (13,409.80 pesos monthly). Although there is no official projection for 2027 yet, it is expected that the percentage increase will be similar to that of the general minimum wage, maintaining the gap between both regions.

What impact would the increase have on workers and the economy?

A minimum wage increase of this magnitude would have direct effects on the income of formal workers earning the base amount, as well as those whose salaries are indexed to the minimum. It could also influence the wage negotiation dynamics in other sectors and the pricing structure of goods and services.

On the other hand, the business sector warns about the risk that higher increments could be passed on to prices, affecting inflation, though recent evidence shows that the increases in previous years have not led to a disproportionate inflationary impact.

When will the minimum wage for 2027 be defined?

The Conasami will initiate formal negotiations in the last week of November 2026 and must publish the official resolution no later than December 1, 2026 . The new minimum wage will come into effect on January 1, 2027 .

Finance Minister Dario Durigan denied on Wednesday (November 18) that the government of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) is working to change the inflation target. According to him, the Brazilian economic environment provides security to attract investments.

Follow the Correio Braziliense channel on WhatsApp and receive the day's top news on your mobile.

"We are not discussing any change to Brazil's inflation target. We have built strong capital markets. We have the right conditions to attract capital and show the world that Brazil is the right place to invest, with commitments to the environment, social commitments, and commitments to democracy," said the head of the economic team during a virtual presentation at the 16th Edition of the Bradesco BBI CEO Forum.

Stay updated on the news that matters to you!

This statement comes amid speculation from government officials that the Executive is planning to raise the target set by the National Monetary Council (CMN) as a strategy for the Central Bank to lower the basic interest rate (Selic), which is currently at 13.75% per year.

While acknowledging speculation regarding changes to the inflation target, Durigan stated that he does not see this debate gaining traction within the PT. "There is no risk of this gaining momentum and becoming a majority position in the party," the minister assured, also denying that President Lula's party had taken a definitive stance on any measures for capital control.

Commitments and Reforms

At the event, Durigan also remarked that the fiscal adjustment of the complementary bill (PLP) currently under discussion in the Senate is not ideal and that fiscal risk is the key factor affecting interest rates. He also noted that fiscal action would be the government's main asset in addressing the Selic.

"The fiscal results, the primary results, which the government can control, have improved over the years. Of course, they are not ideal, and we are not meeting all the expectations that the market imposes on us. Fiscal risk is a fundamental aspect in explaining interest rates, but there are other factors at play," the minister explained.

When citing the government's fiscal projection and the outlook for reducing the Selic, Dario Durigan acknowledged market expectations that Brazil will experience lower growth in Gross Domestic Product (GDP) next year. However, he asserted that this slowdown in growth will not lead to a recession.

Durigan's participation in the Bradesco event came right after a meeting between him and Lula. Their conversation at the Palácio da Alvorada revolved around market expectations regarding who will head the Finance Ministry in Lula's fourth term and the political negotiations for the approval of the fiscal adjustment package in the Senate.

Considered a priority for the government, the proposal outlines mechanisms to limit fiscal spending. Initially expected to be approved by the House yesterday (17), the text faced resistance from opposition lawmakers. However, there are expectations from both the government and Senator Eduardo Braga (MDB-AM), the rapporteur of the matter, to complete the vote today so that, if approved, it can be sent to the Chamber of Deputies.

By Francisco Artur de Lima

1.1 Activities

Southern Copper Corporation, a New York Stock Exchange-listed company, is a leading global producer of copper and other metals, with operations centered in Mexico and Peru. Its core business activities encompass the exploration, mining, smelting, and refining of copper, alongside by-products such as molybdenum, zinc, silver, and gold, which are supplied to industries including construction, electronics, and renewable energy. The company's fastest-growing segments include copper production, fueled by rising demand from electric vehicles and infrastructure development, as well as molybdenum extraction for high-strength alloys in manufacturing. By focusing on operational efficiency and strategic investments in new projects, Southern Copper maintains a competitive edge in the global mining sector, emphasizing sustainable practices to support long-term growth. It is the largest Non ferrous metals sector company by market capitalization among NYSE- and TXSE-listed stocks.

SECTION 1 CORPORATE PROFILE

1.1 Activities

Southern Copper Corporation, a New York Stock Exchange-listed company, is a leading global producer of copper and other metals, with operations centered in Mexico and Peru. Its core business activities encompass the exploration, mining, smelting, and refining of copper, alongside by-products such as molybdenum, zinc, silver, and gold, which are supplied to industries including construction, electronics, and renewable energy. The company's fastest-growing segments include copper production, fueled by rising demand from electric vehicles and infrastructure development, as well as molybdenum extraction for high-strength alloys in manufacturing. By focusing on operational efficiency and strategic investments in new projects, Southern Copper maintains a competitive edge in the global mining sector, emphasizing sustainable practices to support long-term growth. It is the largest Non ferrous metals sector company by market capitalization among NYSE- and TXSE-listed stocks.

Oct 21, 2026: Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE and BVL: SCCO)

Exhibit 99.1

Victor Pedraglio

Bertin Galarreta

Adjusted EBITDA in 9M26 was $8,609.0 million, 56.2% higher than in 9M25. The adjusted EBITDA margin in 9M26 stood at 65.0% versus 57.7% in 9M25.

On a YTD basis, copper production fell 2.9% in 2026 to stand at 693,602 tonnes. This evolution was mainly driven by a decrease in production at our Peruvian mines due to lower ore grades. YoY the Company smelting and refining facilities increased their production by 15.8% and 10.1%, respectively.

On a YTD basis, mined silver production rose 1.5% compared to 2025. Zinc and molybdenum production were down 7.2% and 5.2% in 2026, respectively.

In 9M26, the operating cash cost per pound of copper, net of by-product revenue credits, was $0.01. This represents a decrease of 98.1% compared to the $0.61 reported in 9M25. The 9M26 cash cost decrease was driven by an increase in by-product revenue credits (+53.6%).

In lieu of fractional shares, cash will be distributed to each shareholder who would otherwise have been entitled to receive a fractional share, based on a share price of $197.83, which is the average of the high and low share price on October 15, 2026.

Mr. German Larrea, Chairman of the Board, commenting on the Companys progress and current circumstances, said: "We are very pleased with our strong third-quarter performance, which delivered a record for net sales, adjusted EBITDA and net income. These achievements were thanks to our strategy and disciplined cost control at the operational level.

Our Tia Maria project is reaching half completion this month, and significant goals have been achieved on different construction fronts. As planned, we have finished pre-stripping works at the La Tapada deposit to uncover areas where mineral can be extracted when we begin operations. Simultaneously, work in the dry and wet areas, where most of the solvent extraction and electrowinning activities will be performed, is advancing steadily and according to projected timelines.

Aug 04, 2026: Fresnillo: Interim Results for the six months to 30 June 2026

Fresnillo plc interim results

for the six months to 30 June 2026

Octavio Alvidrez, Chief Executive Officer, commented:

"Fresnillo delivered an exceptional financial performance in the first half of 2026. Through a combination of solid operational execution and cost discipline, we continued to capitalise on the historic strength of precious metals prices, with revenues up 74.7% to US$3.4 billion, driving Gross Profit up 130.7% to US$2.4 billion and strong operating cash flow. Our financial position enabled us to fund the strategic acquisition of Probe Gold, ongoing capex requirements, investment in exploration, and to declare an increased interim dividend of 43.4 cents per share for the period, in accordance with our dividend policy, while maintaining a robust balance sheet.

"Operationally, gold and silver production was in line with our expectations and plans across our mines are progressing well. We saw year-on-year changes from lower grades, a minor delay in the commissioning of the leaching pad XV at Herradura, and weather-related disruptions.

"We remain focused on managing costs within our control by driving efficiencies across our supply chain and advancing key infrastructure projects, including the interconnection of the Jarillas shaft at Saucito.

"Our full-year production guidance remains unchanged, and our high-margin portfolio puts us in a strong position to capitalise on ongoing market tailwinds. The safety and well-being of our people and host communities remain our core priority as we deliver on our strategy for the remainder of 2026."

Jan 22, 2026: Fresnillo completes acquisition of Probe Gold

Fresnillo plc Completes Acquisition of Probe Gold Inc.

Fresnillo plc ("Fresnillo" or "the Company") is pleased to announce the successful completion of its acquisition ("Transaction") of Probe Gold Inc. ("Probe") following receipt of all required shareholder, court and regulatory approvals.

Fresnillo has paid approximately CAD$770 million (approx. US$555 million) in settlement of the transaction consideration funded with existing cash on hand.

Transaction Highlights

Entry into Canada - provides immediate access to the prolific Val d'Or district in Quebec, a world-class mining jurisdiction with established infrastructure and a skilled workforce.

Scale and growth - adds a 10 million oz gold resource base, led by the flagship Novador project - an advanced asset capable of producing 200,000+ oz/year for over a decade.

Exploration upside - includes a 1,798 km2 land package with significant growth potential, including the Detour Gold Quebec project, which will leverage Fresnillo's technical expertise.

Strategic alignment - fits Fresnillo's disciplined M&A strategy by acquiring value-driven, early-stage and advance precious metals exploration projects that complement core operations and the existing portfolio.

The Company maintains its strong financial position and there is no change to Fresnillo's dividend policy as a result of this acquisition.

Octavio Alvidrez, Chief Executive Officer of Fresnillo, commented:

"We are delighted to complete the acquisition of Probe. As we announced previously, this acquisition is consistent with our disciplined approach to M&A and meets our strict criteria of having a sizeable resource base with upside optionality in a region with mining history, skilled personnel, and existing infrastructure. We are excited that our first project outside of Mexico is in Canada, an outstanding mining jurisdiction with a global reputation for responsible development, and in the Val d'Or region with its proud history of mining.

Fresnillo PLC, a leading British-based mining company headquartered in Mexico City, specializes in the exploration, development, and production of precious metals, primarily silver and gold. As one of the world's largest primary silver producers, the company operates several mines in Mexico, including the prolific Fresnillo and Saucito sites, which form the backbone of its operations. Its core activities encompass the full mining lifecycle, from geological exploration to metal processing and sales, with a strong emphasis on sustainable practices and technological innovation. In recent years, Fresnillo's fastest-growing segments have been its gold production initiatives, driven by expansions at assets like the Herradura mine and new projects such as the Juanicipio joint venture, which have capitalized on rising global demand for gold amid economic uncertainties. This strategic focus has bolstered the company's revenue streams, positioning it as a key player in the global metals market while maintaining a commitment to environmental and community responsibilities.
